content.text: A community garden with 20 plot holders produces around 500 to 800 kg of green waste per month in the growing season. Run through a three-bay or windrow system. This gives 150 to 250 kg of finished compost per month. Enough for the site's raised beds with a small surplus for plot holders.

In England. Composting above 5 m³ per week requires either a permit or a registered environmental permit exemption under these regulations. The standard route is Exemption T23, free to register with the Environment Agency. It covers plant material, untreated wood, paper, and cardboard, but not meat, fish, or cooked food. Scotland, Wales, and Northern Ireland have their own rules.
Common C:N problems on shared sites

Community compost bays fill rapidly with grass clippings in summer. Grass clippings have a C:N ratio of around 15:1: far too nitrogen-rich to compost cleanly without browns. A bay full of only grass clippings compacts, goes anaerobic, and produces a smelly slurry rather than compost. The fix is to post clear signage at the bay requiring every load of grass clippings to be accompanied by an equal volume of brown material. Storing bales of straw or bags of cardboard next to the bay gives contributors a practical way to comply.
Managing contributions from multiple plot holders
Designate one bay as the active input bay and close the others to contributions. Rotate input access when the bay is full.

Post an allow/prohibit list at the bay. Allowed: plant trimmings, grass clippings, cardboard, paper, coffee grounds, vegetable kitchen scraps. Prohibited: meat, cooked food, diseased plants, weeds in seed, cat and dog waste.
Assign one volunteer per season to monitor the bay temperature and turn the heap when it drops below 45 degrees Celsius. A rotating monthly rota avoids dependency on one person.
